title: Rate of Reactions
seo_title: Secondary 4 Chemistry: Rate of Reactions Worksheets (O-Level 6092 with Answers)
standard_text: Describe practical methods for measuring the rate of a reaction, including collecting gas and measuring changes in mass or the time for a precipitate to appear; interpret data and graphs from rate experiments; describe and explain the effects of concentration, pressure, surface area (particle size), temperature and catalysts on the rate of reaction in terms of collision theory and activation energy; describe enzymes as biological catalysts (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Chemistry 6092 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 4 O-Level Chemistry worksheets on rate of reactions: measuring rate, rate graphs, collision theory, concentration, surface area, temperature, catalysts and enzymes. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: More effective collisions per second = faster.
key_sub: A catalyst lowers the activation energy and is not used up.
body_html:
How to think about it

Particles react when they collide with enough energy.

  • Rate = amount of product formed (or reactant used) ÷ time. The gradient of a volume-time graph is the rate; it is steepest at the start.
  • Higher concentration, pressure or surface area: more frequent collisions. Higher temperature: more frequent and more energetic collisions.
  • A catalyst gives a pathway with a lower activation energy. It does not change the amount of product.
  • The total amount of product depends only on the limiting reactant.
Example

60 cm³ of gas in 30 s. Average rate?

60 ÷ 30

Answer: 2 cm³/s

Example

Mg powder instead of ribbon, same mass. Graph?

larger surface area: steeper start

same mass of Mg: same final volume

Answer: steeper, same final height

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a catalyst is used up or makes more product.
  • Saying larger lumps react faster.
  • Saying a higher temperature makes more product (it only makes it faster).
  • Explaining temperature only by 'harder collisions' and forgetting the activation energy.

faq.q: How does temperature affect the rate of reaction?
faq.a: At a higher temperature particles move faster, so they collide more often and a larger fraction of collisions have energy at least equal to the activation energy.
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful. It is chemically unchanged at the end.

faq.q: How do you read a rate graph?
faq.a: The steeper the curve, the faster the reaction. Where the curve becomes flat, the reaction has stopped; the final height shows the total amount of product.
